core: working definition of team development, attributed to Tuckman's model as presented by OpenStax's Principles of Management: team development is the process by which a group of people becomes a working team, moving through stages as it matures
the five stages of Tuckman's model: forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning, each with a one-line description and an original example from the lesson's running Northgate co-op scenario
why stages matter: conflict in the early stages is normal and expected, not a sign of failure
stage versus reality: teams loop back, skip stages, and slide backward (regression), for example when a new member joins or a new task creates confusion

the leader's role: different stages need different support, stated simply (direction in forming, open communication and mediation in storming, reinforcement of norms in norming, autonomy in performing, closure in adjourning)
team development and performance: mature teams work more smoothly and need less direction, and the strongest teams optimize both task work and relationships
the honest framing: storming is a stage, not a failure
supporting: historical attribution: Bruce Tuckman, educational psychologist at Ohio State University, published the four-stage model in 1965 and added adjourning in 1977 (OpenStax; Wikipedia corroborates the 1965 date and the 'necessary and inevitable' framing)

stage descriptions: OpenStax calls forming the 'polite stage' and storming the 'win-lose' stage; CFI describes forming as polite and cautious with possible anxiety, and storming as the stage where conflict can be healthy when managed constructively
high-performing team concept: teams that optimize both task and people relationships (OpenStax, citing the Katzenbach-Smith team performance curve idea)
regression triggers: adding a team member or introducing a confusing new task can cause a backwards slide (OpenStax); a new member can take a team back to storming (CFI)
CFI's conclusion that team development is not a linear process and teams may revisit earlier stages as new challenges arise

leader practices by stage: clear direction and role clarification in forming, encouraging open communication and mediating in storming, reinforcing positive behavior in norming, stepping back to allow autonomy in performing, and acknowledging contributions and providing closure in adjourning (CFI; OpenStax adds that forming teams look to the leader for structure and direction while performing teams need little management direction)
outOfScope: teams — the sibling topic owns what a team is, team types, and why organizations use teams; this lesson starts from 'a group becomes a team' and focuses on the development stages
conflict-resolution — the sibling topic owns how to resolve disagreements in depth; storming appears here only as a normal development stage
communication — the sibling topic owns communication skills; mentioned here only as one leader practice (keeping communication open during storming)
performance-management — the sibling topic owns how organizations measure and manage individual performance; the performing stage is a development stage, not a performance-appraisal system
specific team-building exercises, facilitation techniques, and assessment tools — practitioner detail outside this lesson

claims.claim: Team development is the process by which a group of people becomes a working team, moving through stages as it matures; the lesson's working definition follows Tuckman's model as presented in OpenStax's Principles of Management, which describes recognizable stages of team development.

Bruce Tuckman, an educational psychologist at Ohio State University, developed the four-stage model of group development (forming, storming, norming, performing) in 1965 and added the fifth stage, adjourning, in 1977 to explain the disbanding of a team at the end of a project.

Forming is the polite, cautious opening stage: members are introduced, stay on their best behavior, and look to the leader for structure and direction, while enthusiasm mixes with uncertainty about roles and goals.

Storming is the conflict stage: members assert their ideas, test roles and group processes, and clash over goals, tasks, and progress, and frustration builds; sources note conflict at this stage can be healthy when managed constructively.

Norming is the stage when the team starts working well together: buy-in to group goals, established ground rules and boundaries, willingness to share responsibility, and growing respect among members.

Performing is the self-directed stage: the team requires little management direction, has confidence and momentum, and may become a high-performing team that has optimized both task and people relationships.

Adjourning is the closing stage: the team disbands when the project ends, members may feel mixed emotions, and leaders can help by acknowledging contributions, providing closure, and capturing lessons learned.

Team development is not linear: teams can regress or slide back to an earlier stage when a new member joins or a new task creates confusion, and they typically re-form and re-storm before returning to performing.
Tuckman described the phases as necessary and inevitable for a team to grow, face challenges, and deliver results, which underlies the lesson's honest framing that storming is a stage, not a failure.

A leader's support changes by stage: provide structure and direction in forming, encourage open communication and mediate in storming, reinforce positive behavior and norms in norming, step back and allow autonomy in performing, and acknowledge contributions and provide closure in adjourning.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether teams move through the stages in a fixed order
positions: OpenStax presents the model as a sequence of stages but stresses it is not linear: adding a team member or introducing a confusing new task can cause a backwards slide to an earlier stage.

CFI concludes that team development is not a linear process and that teams may revisit earlier stages as new challenges arise, and gives the example of a new member taking a norming team back to storming.
Wikipedia describes the phases as proposed by Tuckman as necessary and inevitable for team growth, without claiming every team experiences them identically or in a fixed schedule.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: No substantive conflict: all sources agree the stages describe a general pattern, not a fixed timetable. This lesson therefore presents the stages as a typical path that real teams loop through, skip, and revisit, and it warns against expecting a clean straight line.

positions: OpenStax emphasizes the negative face of storming: vying for leadership, choosing sides, and frustration around goals, tasks, and progress ('win-lose' stage).

CFI describes storming as increased conflict and competition where differences surface, and adds that conflict can be healthy when managed constructively, leading to better decision-making and cohesion.
Wikipedia's summary notes storming is where the group sorts itself out and gains trust, with conflict arising as power and status are assigned.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The sources differ in emphasis, not in substance: storming involves real friction, and that friction can serve the team when it is managed. The lesson teaches storming as a normal stage where differences surface and get worked through, not as a signal of failure.
